body.en:
Normalization is the process of organizing the columns (attributes) and tables (relations) of a relational database to reduce data redundancy and remove insertion, update and deletion anomalies. A large table is broken into smaller, well-structured tables that are linked by primary key / foreign key relationships.

It was introduced by E. F. Codd (the father of the relational model), who defined 1NF, 2NF and 3NF. Normalization is done step by step using functional dependencies and normal forms.

Objectives (goals)

  • Store each fact only once (minimum redundancy).
  • Remove insertion, update and deletion anomalies.
  • Keep the data consistent and maintain data integrity.
  • Make the design simple, flexible and easy to extend.
  • Make sure the decomposition is lossless: the original data can be rebuilt by joining the tables.

Importance of normalization

  • Saves storage space because repeated data is removed.
  • Data consistency: a value is changed in one place only, so different copies cannot disagree.
  • Easy maintenance: insert, update and delete are simple and safe.
  • Better data integrity through primary and foreign keys.
  • Clear structure: each table describes one entity (student, course, department), which makes the design easier to understand.
  • It is a key step in the logical design of a database (after the E-R diagram is converted into tables).

Data redundancy means the same data is stored repeatedly in a database. In the table STUD_COURSE(ROLL, NAME, CID, CNAME, FEES), the course name and fees are repeated for every student in that course. Redundancy wastes space and causes three kinds of problems called anomalies.

1. Insertion anomaly

We cannot insert some data without inserting other, unrelated data. For example, a new course C3 cannot be stored until at least one student joins it, because ROLL is part of the primary key and cannot be NULL.

2. Update (modification) anomaly

The same fact is stored in many rows, so a change must be made in every row. If even one row is missed, the data becomes inconsistent. For example, the DBMS fee is stored in 3 rows; updating only one row gives two different fees for the same course.

3. Deletion anomaly

Deleting some data unintentionally deletes other useful data. For example, if Isha is the only student of the Python course and her row is deleted, all information about the Python course is also lost.

Cause: one table stores facts about more than one entity (students and courses). Solution: normalization: store students, courses and enrolments in separate tables.

Keys are used to identify rows uniquely and to define normal forms.

  • Super key: a set of one or more attributes that uniquely identifies each row. Example: {ROLL}, {ROLL, NAME}, {EMAIL, CITY}.
  • Candidate key: a minimal super key: no attribute can be removed from it. Example: {ROLL}, {EMAIL}, {AADHAAR}.
  • Primary key: the candidate key chosen by the designer to identify rows. It must be unique and NOT NULL. Example: ROLL.
  • Alternate key: a candidate key that is not chosen as the primary key. Example: EMAIL, AADHAAR.
  • Composite key: a key made of two or more attributes. Example: (ROLL, CID) in RESULT.
  • Foreign key: an attribute that refers to the primary key of another (or the same) table. Example: DEPTNO in EMP refers to DEPT(DEPTNO).

Prime attribute: an attribute that is part of any candidate key. Non-prime (non-key) attribute: an attribute that is not part of any candidate key. These terms are used in the definitions of 2NF and 3NF.

A functional dependency X → Y (read "X determines Y") holds on a relation R if, whenever two rows have the same value of X, they must also have the same value of Y. X is called the determinant and Y the dependent.

In other words, the value of X uniquely decides the value of Y.

Examples (from EMP, DEPT and RESULT):

  • EMPNO → ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO (one employee number gives exactly one name, salary and department).
  • DEPTNO → DNAME, LOC.
  • ROLL, CID → MARKS (a student gets one mark in one course).
  • ENAME → EMPNO does not hold if two employees can have the same name.

FDs come from the meaning of the data (business rules), not from a few sample rows. A sample can only show that an FD does not hold.

Trivial FD: X → Y where Y is a subset of X, e.g. {ROLL, NAME} → NAME. It always holds. Non-trivial FD: Y is not a subset of X, e.g. ROLL → NAME.

Armstrong's axioms are rules for deriving new FDs from given FDs (F). They are sound and complete.

RuleStatement
ReflexivityIf Y ⊆ X, then X → Y
AugmentationIf X → Y, then XZ → YZ
TransitivityIf X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z
Union (derived)If X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ
Decomposition (derived)If X → YZ, then X → Y and X → Z
Pseudo-transitivity (derived)If X → Y and WY → Z, then WX → Z

Attribute closure (X+)

The closure X+ is the set of all attributes that are functionally determined by X using F.

  1. Set result = X.
  2. For each FD A → B in F: if A ⊆ result, add B to result.
  3. Repeat step 2 until result does not change.

Uses: if X+ contains all attributes of R, then X is a super key; if no proper subset of X is a super key, X is a candidate key. It also tests whether an FD X → Y holds (check whether Y ⊆ X+).

Tip: an attribute that never appears on the right side of any FD must be part of every candidate key.

• Full functional dependency: Y depends on the whole of X and not on any proper subset of X. Example: (ROLL, CID) → MARKS, since neither ROLL alone nor CID alone gives the marks.
  • Partial dependency: a non-prime attribute depends on part of a composite candidate key. Example: in RESULT(ROLL, CID, NAME, MARKS), ROLL → NAME. Partial dependencies violate 2NF.
  • Transitive dependency: X → Y and Y → Z, where Y is not a key and Z is non-prime, so X → Z holds indirectly. Example: EMPNO → DEPTNO and DEPTNO → DNAME give EMPNO → DNAME. Transitive dependencies violate 3NF.
  • Trivial / non-trivial dependency: explained in the previous topic.
  • Multivalued dependency (X →→ Y): one X value is associated with a set of Y values independent of other attributes; used in 4NF (beyond syllabus).

A normal form is a condition (set of rules) that a relation must satisfy. Each higher normal form removes one more kind of bad dependency, and each includes all the lower ones:

UNF → 1NF → 2NF → 3NF → BCNF → 4NF → 5NF

Normal formRuleRemoves
1NFAll values atomic; no repeating groupsMulti-valued cells
2NF1NF + no partial dependencyPartial dependency
3NF2NF + no transitive dependencyTransitive dependency
BCNFEvery determinant is a candidate keyRemaining anomalies

The method is decomposition: a relation that breaks a rule is split into two or more relations, each with its own key. In practice, most databases are designed up to 3NF.

An unnormalized form (UNF) table contains repeating groups or multi-valued attributes, e.g. a COURSES column holding "DBMS, OS".

Definition: a relation is in 1NF if every attribute contains only atomic (indivisible) values and there are no repeating groups. Each cell holds a single value of the attribute's domain.

Rules of 1NF

  • Each column holds a single value (no lists such as "DBMS, OS").
  • No repeating groups of columns (COURSE1, COURSE2, COURSE3).
  • All values in a column are of the same type (domain).
  • Each row is unique: a primary key is identified.
  • The order of rows and columns does not matter.

How to convert UNF to 1NF

  1. Flattening: create a separate row for each value of the multi-valued attribute and repeat the other values. The key becomes composite, e.g. (ROLL, COURSE).
  2. Decomposition: move the repeating group to a new table together with a copy of the primary key: STUDENT(ROLL, NAME) and STUDENT_COURSE(ROLL, COURSE).

A table in 1NF can still have redundancy (NAME repeated for each course), which is removed by 2NF.

In Oracle every column of a normal table already holds one value of its data type, so tables created with CREATE TABLE are in 1NF as long as lists are not stored inside VARCHAR2 columns.

Definition: a relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key, i.e. there is no partial dependency.

A partial dependency is possible only when the key is composite. So a 1NF relation whose candidate keys all have a single attribute is automatically in 2NF.

Steps to convert 1NF to 2NF

  1. Find the candidate key(s) and the FDs.
  2. Find each partial dependency (part of key → non-prime attributes).
  3. Move each partial dependency into a new table; the part of the key becomes the primary key of the new table.
  4. Keep the attributes that depend on the whole key in the original table with the full key.

Example: RESULT(ROLL, CID, NAME, CNAME, MARKS) with key (ROLL, CID). ROLL → NAME and CID → CNAME are partial. 2NF tables: STUDENT(ROLL, NAME), COURSE(CID, CNAME), RESULT(ROLL, CID, MARKS).

A 2NF table can still have transitive dependencies, which are removed by 3NF.

Definition: a relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.

Formal definition: for every non-trivial FD X → A, either X is a super key or A is a prime attribute.

In simple words: "every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."

Steps to convert 2NF to 3NF

  1. Find each transitive dependency: key → Y → Z, where Y is a non-key attribute.
  2. Move Y and the attributes it determines (Z) into a new table with Y as the primary key.
  3. Keep Y in the original table as a foreign key.

Example: EMPLOYEE(EMPNO, ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO, DNAME, LOC) has EMPNO → DEPTNO → DNAME, LOC. 3NF tables: EMP(EMPNO, ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO) and DEPT(DEPTNO, DNAME, LOC). This is exactly how the EMP and DEPT tables of the SCOTT schema are designed.

In SQL, an existing table can be split with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT DISTINCT:

CREATE TABLE dept3 AS
SELECT DISTINCT deptno, dname, loc
FROM emp_flat;

BCNF is a stronger version of 3NF. A relation is in BCNF if for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a super key. That is, every determinant must be a candidate key.

3NF allows X → A when A is a prime attribute; BCNF does not. So every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but a 3NF relation may not be in BCNF.

Example: TEACH(STUDENT, SUBJECT, TEACHER), where each teacher teaches only one subject (TEACHER → SUBJECT) and (STUDENT, SUBJECT) → TEACHER. The candidate keys are (STUDENT, SUBJECT) and (STUDENT, TEACHER), so all attributes are prime and the relation is in 3NF. But TEACHER is not a super key, so it is not in BCNF. Decompose into (TEACHER, SUBJECT) and (STUDENT, TEACHER).

BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may not preserve all dependencies, which is why 3NF is often accepted in practice.

Normalization of a real table is done in a fixed order. Write down the FDs first, then apply each normal form in turn.

  1. UNF → 1NF: remove repeating groups; make every value atomic; find the primary key.
  2. 1NF → 2NF: remove partial dependencies (part of key → non-key).
  3. 2NF → 3NF: remove transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key).
  4. Check: each final table has a primary key; foreign keys link the tables; a natural join of the tables gives back the original data (lossless).

A student-course database, for example, ends with three tables: STUDENT(ROLL, NAME), COURSE(CID, CNAME, FEES) and ENROLL(ROLL, CID). A new course can be added without students, a fee is changed in one row, and deleting an enrolment never deletes course data.

The worked examples below show a complete order bill normalized to four tables, and an abstract relation normalized step by step.

Advantages

  • Less redundancy: each fact is stored only once, which saves storage.
  • No anomalies: insertion, update and deletion anomalies are removed.
  • Data consistency and integrity: one copy of the data cannot disagree with itself; keys enforce relationships.
  • Easier maintenance: changes are made in one place.
  • Better design: each table represents one entity, so the database is easy to understand and extend.
  • Smaller tables: indexes and searches on small tables are faster, and fewer NULL values are stored.
  • Flexible queries: data can be combined in many ways using joins.

Disadvantages

  • More tables: the number of tables increases, so the design looks complex.
  • More joins: queries need joins to combine data, which can reduce performance for reports.
  • Harder to write queries for beginners.
  • Requires skill: correct FDs and keys must be identified; this takes time and a good understanding of the data.
  • Over-normalization (beyond 3NF / BCNF) may give little benefit for extra complexity.

h.en: Decomposition: Lossless Join and Dependency Preservation

body.en:
Decomposition means replacing a relation R by two or more relations R1, R2, ... such that every attribute of R appears in at least one of them. A good decomposition has two properties.

1. Lossless-join decomposition

Joining R1 and R2 gives back exactly the original R: no rows are lost and no extra (spurious) rows appear. Test: the decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if the common attributes R1 ∩ R2 form a key (super key) of R1 or of R2.

Example: EMP(EMPNO, ENAME, DEPTNO) and DEPT(DEPTNO, DNAME, LOC). The common attribute DEPTNO is the key of DEPT, so the decomposition is lossless. Splitting into (EMPNO, ENAME) and (DNAME, LOC) would be lossy, because there is no common attribute to join on.

2. Dependency-preserving decomposition

Every FD of the original relation can be checked within a single decomposed relation (or derived from the FDs of the decomposed relations), so constraints can be enforced without joins.

Decomposition into 3NF can always be done so that it is both lossless and dependency-preserving. BCNF is always lossless but may not preserve all dependencies.

Denormalization is the deliberate process of adding some redundancy back into a normalized database (for example, combining tables or storing calculated values) to improve read (query) performance.

When it is used: reporting systems and data warehouses, where data is read far more often than it is updated, and joining many tables is slow.

Examples:

  • Storing DNAME in an EMP report table to avoid joining DEPT.
  • Storing a TOTAL_AMOUNT column in ORDERS instead of summing ORDER_ITEM rows every time.
NormalizationDenormalization
Removes redundancyAdds controlled redundancy
More tables, more joinsFewer tables, fewer joins
Faster insert, update and deleteFaster SELECT (reports)
Better consistencyRisk of inconsistency
Used in OLTP (transaction) systemsUsed in OLAP / data warehouses

Denormalization is done after normalization, never instead of it.

expl.en:
• The course details (CNAME, FEES) are repeated for every student who joins the course, and Aarav's name is repeated for each of his courses: this is redundancy.
  • The new DBMS fee was saved in only one of the three DBMS rows. Now the same course C1 shows two different fees (5000 and 5500): an update anomaly, which makes the data inconsistent.
  • Only the dependency CID → CNAME, FEES caused this. Normalization moves it into its own table.

2 rows deleted.

--- ----- ----
C1  DBMS  5000

expl.en:
• Insertion anomaly: to store a new course we must insert a row with NULL roll and name. If (ROLL, CID) were the primary key, this insert would be rejected, because a key cannot be NULL.
  • Deletion anomaly: deleting the only students of course C2 also deleted all information about C2 (its name and fees). The course has disappeared from the database.

  • A new course can be added without any student, so there is no insertion anomaly.
  • The DBMS fee is changed with a single-row update, so there is no update anomaly.
  • Deleting an enrolment from ENROLL never deletes course data, so there is no deletion anomaly.

title.en: Join the 3NF tables to get the original data back

code.en:
SELECT e.roll, s.name, e.cid,
       c.cname, c.fees
FROM enroll e
JOIN student s ON e.roll = s.roll
JOIN course c ON e.cid = c.cid
ORDER BY e.roll, e.cid;

SELECT c.cname, COUNT(e.roll) students
FROM course c LEFT JOIN enroll e
ON c.cid = e.cid
GROUP BY c.cname
ORDER BY c.cname;

  • The second query counts the students in each course. The LEFT JOIN keeps courses that have no students.

title.en: Normalize an existing table using CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT

code.en:
-- emp_flat repeats dname and loc
CREATE TABLE emp_flat AS
SELECT e.empno, e.ename, e.deptno,
       d.dname, d.loc
FROM emp e JOIN dept d
ON e.deptno = d.deptno;

-- 3NF: move DEPTNO -> DNAME, LOC out
CREATE TABLE dept3 AS
SELECT DISTINCT deptno, dname, loc
FROM emp_flat;

CREATE TABLE emp3 AS
SELECT empno, ename, deptno
FROM emp_flat;

SELECT * FROM dept3 ORDER BY deptno;

SELECT COUNT(*) flat_rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT deptno) depts
FROM emp_flat;

q.en:
Convert the following unnormalized STUDENT table into 1NF.
ROLLNAMECITYCOURSES
1AaravSuratDBMS, OS
2DiyaVadodaraDBMS
3KaranRajkotOS, CN, Java

a.en:
Why it is not in 1NF: the COURSES column holds several values in one cell (a multi-valued / repeating group). 1NF requires every cell to hold a single atomic value.

Method 1 (flattening): write one row for each course.

ROLLNAMECITYCOURSE
1AaravSuratDBMS
1AaravSuratOS
2DiyaVadodaraDBMS
3KaranRajkotOS
3KaranRajkotCN
3KaranRajkotJava

Primary key = (ROLL, COURSE), because ROLL alone repeats. The table is now in 1NF, but NAME and CITY repeat (redundancy), so it needs 2NF.

Method 2 (decomposition): move the repeating group to a separate table:

STUDENT(ROLL, NAME, CITY)
STUDENT_COURSE(ROLL, COURSE)

Method 2 already removes the redundancy and gives tables in 3NF.

q.en:
RESULT(ROLL, CID, NAME, CNAME, CREDITS, MARKS) has the functional dependencies:
ROLL → NAME
CID → CNAME, CREDITS
ROLL, CID → MARKS
Find the key and convert the relation into 2NF.

a.en:
Step 1: Candidate key. (ROLL, CID)+ = {ROLL, CID, NAME, CNAME, CREDITS, MARKS} = all attributes, and neither ROLL nor CID alone determines everything. So the key is (ROLL, CID) (composite).

Step 2: Check 2NF. Non-key attributes: NAME, CNAME, CREDITS, MARKS.

  • ROLL → NAME: NAME depends on part of the key → partial dependency.
  • CID → CNAME, CREDITS: partial dependency.
  • ROLL, CID → MARKS: full dependency (OK).

Because of the partial dependencies, RESULT is in 1NF only.

Step 3: Decompose. Put each partial dependency in a separate table with its determinant as the key, and keep the full dependency with the whole key:

STUDENT(ROLL, NAME)
COURSE(CID, CNAME, CREDITS)
RESULT(ROLL, CID, MARKS)

ROLL and CID in RESULT are foreign keys. All three tables are in 2NF (in fact in 3NF, since no transitive dependency remains).

q.en:
EMPLOYEE(EMPNO, ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO, DNAME, LOC) with FDs:
EMPNO → ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO
DEPTNO → DNAME, LOC
Is it in 3NF? If not, normalize it to 3NF.

a.en:
Key: EMPNO+ = {EMPNO, ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO} → using DEPTNO → DNAME, LOC → {all six attributes}. So EMPNO is the key.

2NF? The key has only one attribute, so a partial dependency is impossible. EMPLOYEE is in 2NF.

3NF? DEPTNO → DNAME, LOC: a non-key attribute (DEPTNO) determines other non-key attributes. Since EMPNO → DEPTNO and DEPTNO → DNAME, we get EMPNO → DNAME transitively. So it is not in 3NF.

Problem: DNAME and LOC are repeated for every employee of the department (update anomaly), and a department without employees cannot be stored (insertion anomaly).

Decompose:

EMP(EMPNO, ENAME, SAL, DEPTNO) (DEPTNO is a foreign key)
DEPT(DEPTNO, DNAME, LOC)

Both tables are in 3NF. Joining EMP and DEPT on DEPTNO gives back the original table (lossless decomposition).

q.en:
Normalize the following customer order (bill) data up to 3NF.
ONOODATECIDCNAMECITYITEMS (ICODE, INAME, RATE, QTY)
50105-OCT-26C1Mehta StoresSuratI1 Pen 10 x5; I2 Book 60 x2
50206-OCT-26C2Shah TradersAnandI1 Pen 10 x3

a.en:
UNF → 1NF. The ITEMS column is a repeating group. Make one row per item (atomic values):

ONOODATECIDCNAMECITYICODEINAMERATEQTY
50105-OCT-26C1Mehta StoresSuratI1Pen105
50105-OCT-26C1Mehta StoresSuratI2Book602
50206-OCT-26C2Shah TradersAnandI1Pen103

Functional dependencies:

  • ONO → ODATE, CID
  • CID → CNAME, CITY
  • ICODE → INAME, RATE
  • ONO, ICODE → QTY

Key = (ONO, ICODE), since (ONO, ICODE)+ gives all nine attributes.

1NF → 2NF. Partial dependencies: ONO → ODATE, CID (and so CNAME, CITY) and ICODE → INAME, RATE. Remove them:

ORDER_ITEM(ONO, ICODE, QTY)
ITEM(ICODE, INAME, RATE)
ORDERS(ONO, ODATE, CID, CNAME, CITY)

2NF → 3NF. In ORDERS, ONO → CID → CNAME, CITY is a transitive dependency. Split ORDERS:

ORDERS(ONO, ODATE, CID)
CUSTOMER(CID, CNAME, CITY)

Final 3NF design (4 tables): CUSTOMER, ORDERS, ITEM and ORDER_ITEM. Customer and item details are now stored only once; the amount of a line is calculated as RATE × QTY when needed.

q.en: R(A, B, C, D) with F = { AB → C, C → D }. Find the candidate key and the highest normal form. Decompose into 3NF if needed.

a.en:
Closure of AB:
Start: {A, B}
A, B → C gives {A, B, C}
C → D gives {A, B, C, D}
AB+ contains all attributes, so AB is a super key. A+ = {A} and B+ = {B}, so AB is minimal: candidate key = AB.

Prime attributes: A, B. Non-prime: C, D.

2NF: does any non-prime attribute depend on only A or only B? No (A+ and B+ contain nothing else). So R is in 2NF.

3NF: C → D: C is not a super key and D is non-prime. AB → C → D is a transitive dependency. So R is not in 3NF; the highest normal form is 2NF.

Decomposition: R1(A, B, C) and R2(C, D). In R1 the only FD is AB → C, and in R2 it is C → D; both left sides are keys, so both are in 3NF (and BCNF). The common attribute C is the key of R2, so the decomposition is lossless.

q.en: R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = { A → B, AC → D, D → E }. Find the key, the normal form, and normalize R up to 3NF.

a.en:
Key: A and C never appear on the right side of any FD, so both must be in every key.
Start: {A, C}
A → B gives {A, B, C}
A, C → D gives {A, B, C, D}
D → E gives {A, B, C, D, E}
AC+ = all attributes, so AC is the candidate key.

Check:

  • A → B: B depends on part (A) of the key → partial dependency. So R is only in 1NF.
  • D → E: E depends on the non-key attribute D → transitive dependency.

To 2NF: remove the partial dependency: R1(A, B) and R2(A, C, D, E).

To 3NF: in R2, AC → D → E is transitive. Split R2 into R21(A, C, D) and R22(D, E).

Final 3NF relations: R1(A, B), R21(A, C, D), R22(D, E).

q.en: R(A, B, C, D, E) with F = { A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A }. Compute A<sup>+</sup>, E<sup>+</sup>, (BC)<sup>+</sup>, (CD)<sup>+</sup> and find all candidate keys.

a.en:
Attribute closure algorithm: start with the given attributes; repeatedly, for every FD X → Y whose left side X is already in the result, add Y; stop when nothing changes.

A+:
Start: {A}
A → B, C gives {A, B, C}
B → D gives {A, B, C, D}
C, D → E gives {A, B, C, D, E}
A+ = ABCDE → A is a key.

E+:
Start: {E}
E → A gives {A, E}
A → B, C gives {A, B, C, E}
B → D gives {A, B, C, D, E}
E+ = ABCDE → E is a key.

(BC)+:
Start: {B, C}
B → D gives {B, C, D}
C, D → E gives {B, C, D, E}
E → A gives {A, B, C, D, E}
→ BC is a super key. B+ = {B, D} and C+ = {C}, so BC is minimal: candidate key.

(CD)+:
Start: {C, D}
C, D → E gives {C, D, E}
E → A gives {A, C, D, E}
A → B, C gives {A, B, C, D, E}
→ CD is a super key; C+ = {C}, D+ = {D}, so CD is a candidate key.

Candidate keys: A, E, BC and CD. Prime attributes = A, B, C, D, E (all), so there are no non-prime attributes and R is in 3NF.
The process of organizing tables and columns to reduce redundancy and remove insertion, update and deletion anomalies, by decomposing large tables into smaller related tables.
Dr. E. F. Codd, the father of the relational model.
Storing the same data more than once in a database.
Insertion anomaly, update (modification) anomaly and deletion anomaly.
Some data cannot be inserted without other unrelated data, e.g. a new course cannot be added until a student joins it.
The same fact is stored in many rows; if one copy is not updated, the data becomes inconsistent.
Deleting one fact unintentionally removes another, e.g. deleting the last student of a course also loses the course details.
A minimal super key: a set of attributes that uniquely identifies rows, with no unnecessary attribute.

q.en: What is the difference between a super key and a candidate key?

a.en: Every candidate key is a super key, but a super key may contain extra attributes. A candidate key is minimal.
A key made of two or more attributes, e.g. (ROLL, CID).
An attribute that is part of at least one candidate key. Others are non-prime attributes.
X → Y means that the value of X uniquely determines the value of Y: rows with the same X always have the same Y.

q.en: In X → Y, what are X and Y called?

a.en: X is the determinant and Y is the dependent.

q.en: What is a trivial functional dependency?

a.en: X → Y where Y is a subset of X, e.g. {ROLL, NAME} → ROLL.

q.en: What is a full functional dependency?

a.en: Y depends on the whole composite key X and not on any part of it, e.g. (ROLL, CID) → MARKS.
A non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key, e.g. ROLL → NAME when the key is (ROLL, CID).
If X → Y and Y → Z, where Y is non-key, then Z depends on X transitively, e.g. EMPNO → DEPTNO → DNAME.
Reflexivity (if Y ⊆ X then X → Y), augmentation (if X → Y then XZ → YZ) and transitivity (if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z).
X<sup>+</sup> is the set of all attributes that can be determined from X using the given FDs.

q.en: How do you find whether X is a super key?

a.en: Compute X<sup>+</sup>; if it contains all attributes of the relation, X is a super key.
A set of rules (conditions) a relation must satisfy to reduce redundancy and anomalies.
A relation is in 1NF if every attribute holds only atomic (single) values and there are no repeating groups.
A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and has no partial dependency: every non-prime attribute fully depends on the whole key.
A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and has no transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on the key.
A relation is in BCNF if, for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a super key (every determinant is a candidate key).

q.en: When is a 1NF table automatically in 2NF?

a.en: When every candidate key has only one attribute, because a partial dependency needs a composite key.
No. Every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but a 3NF relation may have a determinant that is not a key (for a prime attribute).

q.en: Which normal form is usually enough in practice?

a.en: 3NF (sometimes BCNF).
Unnormalized form: a table with repeating groups or multi-valued cells.
By decomposition: splitting a table that breaks a rule into smaller tables, each with its own primary key, linked by foreign keys.
Less redundancy (saves space) and no anomalies (consistent data).
More tables, and more joins are needed in queries, which can slow down reports.
A decomposition in which joining the smaller tables gives back exactly the original table, with no lost or extra rows.

q.en: How do you test that a decomposition into R1 and R2 is lossless?

a.en: The common attributes of R1 and R2 must be a key of R1 or of R2.
Every original FD can be checked within the decomposed tables without joining them.
Deliberately adding controlled redundancy to a normalized database to make queries faster.
In reporting systems and data warehouses (OLAP), where reads are much more frequent than updates.

What is functional dependency? Explain full, partial and transitive dependency with examples.

R(A,B,C,D) with AB → C and C → D. Find the key and the highest normal form, and decompose into 3NF.

Explain the advantages and disadvantages of normalization.
